output.rationale: This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (along with PM10) exposure and respiratory hospital admissions using distributed lag non-linear models, which is a time-series approach. The study reports quantitative associations and risk estimates for respiratory diseases including asthma and COPD. While the focus is on comparing pre- and post-COVID periods, it meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with statistical significance.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (asthma exacerbations) using what appears to be a time-series design (mixed-effects quasi-Poisson regression with daily data). However, the abstract does not explicitly report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. It only mentions statistical significance (P<10-4) and describes a non-linear sigmoid relationship. Without confirmation that quantitative effect estimates with CIs are reported in the full text, the decision remains uncertain.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 as exposure, (3) outcome is asthma hospitalization which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) uses case-crossover design (time-stratified), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (0.31% increase per 1-μg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 0.24-0.37%), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between PM2.5 (as the primary component of AQI) and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits for childhood asthma. The study reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary exposure is AQI, the abstract explicitly states that PM2.5 was the primary pollutant responsible for the AQI (62% of days) and that the association was strongest for PM2.5-specific AQI. The outcome is asthma exacerbations resulting in ED visits and hospitalizations, which meets the respiratory hospitalization/ED visit criterion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations (32 respiratory discharge diagnoses), (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect measures) for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes with positive associations reported for 31 of 32 respiratory outcomes, and (6) the publication appears to be in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as a major outcome category.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis with DLNM; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for respiratory disease; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) it reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR=1.030, 95% CI: 1.012-1.049 for PM2.5); and (6) the article is published in English. Although multiple air pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported with quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome includes both respiratory ED presentations and hospitalizations for bronchiolitis, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with quantitative effect estimates (>10% increased risk for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. While multiple pollutants are examined (NO2, PM10, PM2.5), PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures examined, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (acute upper respiratory infections), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR=1.0247, 95% CI: 1.0092-1.0405), and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and emergency department visits, (4) study design is case-crossover as explicitly stated, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the population is specific (childhood cancer survivors), this does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10 and NO2), reports respiratory hospitalizations (bronchiolitis) as the outcome, and provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. The study is published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates for PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes fine particulate matter (PM2.5), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations in children, (4) study design is case-crossover, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR=1.004 [0.955-1.056] overall and stratified estimates), and (6) appears to be published in English. Although the study also examines oxidant gases and particle constituents as effect modifiers, PM2.5 is clearly one of the primary exposures analyzed.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with effect estimates, original research), the outcome is hospitalization specifically for SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 infection rather than general respiratory hospitalizations. COVID-19 hospitalizations represent a specific infectious disease outcome that differs from the broader category of respiratory hospitalizations typically examined in PM2.5 systematic reviews. The review appears to focus on general respiratory hospitalizations, not disease-specific infectious outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) uses time-series methodology with quasi-Poisson models, (5) reports rate ratios with 95% credible intervals (e.g., RR=1.016, 95% CI: 1.008-1.025 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English in a peer-reviewed journal (Environmental Health Perspectives).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory ED presentations and hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports incidence rate ratios with 95% CIs (e.g., IRR 1.043, 95% CI: 1.000-1.089 for ED presentations), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) the study design is time-series, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (e.g., increased risk percentages and relative risk mentioned), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and temperature, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalizations, (4) time-series analysis with GAM was used, (5) the results indicate that effect estimates were calculated (PM2.5 and PM10 were 'associated with increased risks'), and (6) the article is in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the numerical effect estimates with confidence intervals, it clearly indicates they were calculated and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire smoke PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (acute respiratory infections, pneumonia, COPD, asthma, and other respiratory diseases), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports relative risk with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes multiple respiratory hospitalization outcomes which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using generalized additive Poisson model, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (URTI hospital admissions) and ED visits, (4) time-series design analyzing daily data, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (0.84% increase per 10 μg/m³, 95% CI 0.05-1.64%), and (6) published in English. Upper respiratory tract infections are respiratory conditions requiring hospitalization.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD. It reports quantitative risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 exposure. Although the main finding was for NO2, PM2.5 was explicitly analyzed and reported with effect estimates (RR for asthma: 0.981-1.148; RR for COPD: 0.966-1.019). The study meets all inclusion criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, quantitative effect estimates with CI, English language), it fails the study design criterion. The abstract explicitly states this is a 'retrospective cohort study' using distributed lag models, not a time-series or case-crossover design as required by the inclusion criteria.

While this is an original epidemiological study with PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke), time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary outcomes are cardiovascular and cerebrovascular ED visits, not respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. Although respiratory conditions are mentioned as a secondary finding, the study's focus and design are centered on cardiovascular/cerebrovascular outcomes, making it inappropriate for a systematic review specifically on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory ED visits (pneumonia, COPD/asthma). It uses a time-series design with distributed lag models and quasi-Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) for respiratory outcomes including pneumonia. Although it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it meets all inclusion criteria for the respiratory component.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory (pneumonia) hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, it uses a prospective cohort design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover design. The inclusion criteria specifically limit eligible study designs to time-series or case-crossover studies only.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory emergency room visits using a generalized additive model (consistent with time-series design). The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR = 1.011, 95%CI: 1.002, 1.020). The outcome is respiratory emergency department visits, which meets the inclusion criteria for respiratory hospitalization/ED visits. The exposure is clearly PM2.5, including both total and source-specific PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure among multiple pollutants, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) reports percentage change in odds with 95% CI (equivalent to OR), and (6) published in English. The study reports a 1.2% increase in odds of admission per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with confidence intervals.

While this is an original time-series study with PM2.5 exposure and quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is hospitalization for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD), which is a specific autoimmune/rheumatologic condition with respiratory manifestations, not general respiratory hospitalization. The review targets respiratory hospitalizations (e.g., asthma, COPD, pneumonia, general respiratory conditions), not hospitalizations for autoimmune diseases that happen to affect the lungs.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory ED visits as outcomes (asthma/wheeze, bronchitis, pneumonia, upper respiratory infections), provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and is published in English in a peer-reviewed journal.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 exposure explicitly stated, (3) respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma and COPD, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CI (e.g., ER = 2.1%, 95% CI = 0.7%, 3.6%), and (6) appears to be in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

While the title mentions 'hospitalization', the abstract clearly describes the outcome as 'outpatient visits' for upper respiratory tract infections, not hospitalizations or ED visits. The study uses a generalized additive model (time-series design) and examines PM2.5 exposure, but does not meet the outcome criteria of respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visit.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using Poisson regression; (2) Exposure is PM2.5; (3) Outcomes include both respiratory ED visits and hospitalizations; (4) Study design is time-series (daily county-level counts linked with daily PM2.5); (5) Reports multiple RR estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory outcomes (e.g., RR=1.25 [1.21, 1.30] for respiratory disease EDVs, RR=1.18 [1.10, 1.27] for CLRD); (6) Published in English. The study examines both ED visits and hospitalizations for respiratory conditions in relation to PM2.5 exposure.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for AECOPD. It reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI) and meets all inclusion criteria. While the study focuses on interaction effects with temperature and includes multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, and AECOPD hospitalizations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.61% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI = 0.87, 2.35%), and (6) published in English. The use of predicted rather than measured PM2.5 does not disqualify the study as it still examines the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for influenza and pneumonia, (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports excess rates with 95% CIs (e.g., ER=9.2%, 95% CI: 4.3%, 14.3%), and (6) published in English. While the study examines source-specific PM2.5 rather than total PM2.5, PM2.5 is the primary exposure being analyzed.

This is an original time-series study using generalized additive models examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for upper respiratory tract infection. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (5.302% increase, 95% CI: 3.202, 7.445 per 10 ug/m3). URTI is a respiratory condition requiring ED visits, meeting the outcome criteria. All inclusion criteria are satisfied.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a generalized additive model, which is characteristic of time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia and asthma) in children; (4) the study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag structure analyzing daily hospitalization rates); (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (2.22% increase per 10-unit PM2.5 increase, 95%CI: 0.64%, 3.82%); and (6) the article is published in English. While multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included and reported separately.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is asthma emergency room admissions which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (7.2% increase, 95% CI 1.7-13.1%), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study with case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures assessed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (ILD admissions are respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% CIs for multiple pollutants including PM2.5, and (6) published in English. While the abstract primarily reports results for SO2 and NO2, PM2.5 was measured and analyzed as stated in the methods.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations and includes PM2.5 as an exposure variable, the abstract does not report any effect estimates (RR or OR with CI) specifically for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The results section only reports associations for NO2, ozone, and noise with various outcomes, but PM2.5 results are not presented despite being listed as a main independent variable in the methods.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (generalized additive model with distributed lag models) examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (COPD admissions). The study reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases in daily admissions). While the abstract shows percentage increases rather than RR/OR format, these can be converted to relative risks. The study meets all major inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) it uses a case-crossover design, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (1.73% increase, 95% CI: 1.34%, 2.12% for PM2.5), and (6) it is published in English. Although it also examines PM2.5-10, PM2.5 is explicitly included as a separate exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original ecological time-series study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, acute bronchitis, bronchiolitis, asthma), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risk estimates with values (RR = 1.017, 1.022, 1.020 at different lags), and (6) published in English. All key elements required for inclusion are clearly present.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospital admissions with quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI). However, the study design is a difference-in-differences approach with distributed lag non-linear models, which is not a standard time-series or case-crossover design as specified in the inclusion criteria. While it uses time-series data (daily PM2.5 and admissions), the analytical approach differs from conventional time-series methods. This warrants expert judgment on whether this methodological variation should be included in the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for respiratory diseases (COPD and upper respiratory diseases), (4) uses a case-crossover study design, (5) reports positive associations (effect estimates) for PM2.5 with various lag periods, and (6) published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state the numerical values of effect estimates, it clearly indicates that quantitative associations were tested and positive results were found for PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization for acute lower respiratory infections including pneumonia, COPD exacerbations, and bronchitis, (4) study design is explicitly stated as time-series, (5) reports percent increases with 95% confidence intervals that can be converted to relative risks, and (6) published in English.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and hospital admissions across multiple disease categories, including respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (e.g., percent increase in admissions per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, respiratory diseases are explicitly included as one of the major disease categories analyzed, making it eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and asthma emergency room visits. It uses generalized additive model with Poisson regression on daily counts of ERVs, reports relative risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 effects on respiratory (asthma) emergency department visits. Although the study also examines PM2.5-bound PAHs, it explicitly reports PM2.5 effects separately and meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) the outcome is hospital admissions for respiratory diseases, (4) it uses a time-series design with generalized additive model, (5) it reports percentage change with 95% CI (PM2.5: 0.755%; 95% CI: 0.422, 1.089% per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) the abstract is in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure, (3) outcome is asthma-related emergency department visits (AEDv), which are respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates (RR with percent increase) are reported for PM2.5 (4.4% increase per IQR), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is one of them with specific effect estimates provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital admissions and emergency department visits (respiratory hospitalizations), (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) the abstract mentions positive associations and 95% confidence intervals indicating effect estimates were reported, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and effect modification, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed as an exposure of interest.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using a time-series design (GAM). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospital admissions (1.03% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI: 0.50%-1.56%). Although the study examines multiple outcomes beyond respiratory hospitalizations, it meets all inclusion criteria for the systematic review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other particle metrics) and hospital admissions including respiratory outcomes. While the abstract emphasizes cardiovascular results, it explicitly states that secondary pollutants including PM2.5 were important for respiratory outcomes. The study uses Poisson regression time-series analysis and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals. It examines emergency hospital admissions which meets the outcome criteria.

This is an original time-series study using GAMs that examines PM2.5 exposure and multiple health outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for respiratory system diseases (NO2: 1.36%, 95%CI: 0.74-1.98%). Although the study examines multiple pollutants and multiple disease categories, it meets all inclusion criteria: it includes PM2.5 as an exposure, respiratory hospitalizations as one of the outcomes, uses a time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization and ED visits for asthma exacerbations, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports relative risk with 95% CI for PM2.5 exposure, and (6) published in English. The study specifically reports RR values for PM2.5 at different lag periods for both ED admissions and hospitalizations.

Although this is a time-series study examining respiratory ED visits with effect estimates reported, and PM2.5 was included as a covariate in the analysis, the primary exposure of interest is thunderstorm-related climate parameters (precipitation and temperature), not PM2.5. The results explicitly state that PM2.5 levels were not significantly associated with asthma ED visits on thunderstorm days, and no effect estimates for PM2.5 are reported. PM2.5 was only used as a control variable in the model, not as the main exposure being investigated.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design with generalized additive model; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (acute lower respiratory tract infections including pneumonia and bronchitis); (4) the study design is time-series; (5) relative risks with 95% confidence intervals are reported for PM2.5 (RR=1.0064, 95% CI 1.0004-1.0124 for pneumonia at lag4 and RR=1.0133, 95% CI 1.0025-1.0242 for bronchitis at lag010); and (6) the abstract is in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), reports respiratory hospitalizations for asthma and COPD as outcomes, provides odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and appears to be published in English.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (along with UFP) exposure and respiratory hospital admissions using a time-series design with Poisson regression. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (relative risk) with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and respiratory admissions (7.5% [4.9-10.2%] per 12.4 μg/m3 increase). All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) time-series study design using Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (percentage increases in hospitalization rates per 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 with specific values: 8.6% for Black individuals, 6.2% for White individuals, 4.1% overall), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (1.74% increase per 10-μg/m3, 95% CI: 1.41-2.07% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (159,365 respiratory disease admissions), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.95% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory diseases, 95% CI 1.63-2.27%), and (6) published in English. The study examines both cardiovascular and respiratory outcomes, but respiratory hospitalizations are explicitly analyzed and reported.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is particle oxidative potential (OP), not PM2.5 mass concentration itself. The study uses PM2.5 as a carrier to express OP measures (OP per μg of PM multiplied by PM concentration), but the exposure of interest and the reported associations are for oxidative potential metrics (OP(AA) and OP(GSH)), not standard PM2.5 mass concentration. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma. It uses a time-series design with Poisson generalized linear models and reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals. All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using GAM for time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure, (3) respiratory disease hospitalization is the outcome, (4) GAM indicates a time-series design, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 1.95% increase with 95% CI: 0.25, 3.67 per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) the abstract is in English. The study provides specific relative risk estimates for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (specifically asthma hospitalizations are reported), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., RR 1.16, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.35 for asthma), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports respiratory hospitalization outcomes which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is chronic respiratory disease (CRD) hospitalizations, (4) time-series design clearly stated, (5) reports excess risks with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (2.13%, 95% CI: 0.55%, 3.74% per 10 μg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 results are specifically reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory healthcare visits (which includes hospitalizations/ED visits), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with effect estimates for PM2.5 increases, and (6) published in English. While the abstract uses the term 'healthcare visits' rather than explicitly stating 'hospitalization' or 'ED visit', respiratory healthcare encounters in this context typically refer to hospital-based care.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is hospitalization for respiratory diseases, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (OR=1.017, 95%CI: 1.003-1.031 for PM2.5), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per the inclusion criteria.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other exposures) and respiratory outcomes including ED visits and hospitalizations (inpatient visits) for asthma exacerbation. The study reports rate ratios with confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on effect modification by viral infections and the main results presented are for pollen, the abstract indicates PM2.5 was analyzed as an exposure and asthma-related ED and inpatient visits are respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

This is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design (GAM with daily data) that examines PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (in patients with comorbid diabetes). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (7.25% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5). While the population is restricted to patients with diabetes and comorbid respiratory diseases, the outcome is still respiratory hospitalization, meeting the inclusion criteria.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, time-series design, PM2.5 exposure, reports RR with CI), the outcome is acute upper respiratory tract infections (AURTIs), which typically refers to infections of the nose, sinuses, pharynx, and larynx (common cold, pharyngitis, sinusitis). These are generally distinct from lower respiratory conditions that typically require hospitalization (pneumonia, COPD exacerbations, asthma). The systematic review focuses on respiratory hospitalizations, which conventionally refers to more severe lower respiratory conditions rather than upper respiratory tract infections.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using generalized additive models, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) it uses a time-series study design as stated in the title and methods, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 6.1% increase, CI: 2.1-10.3%), and (6) the article is in English. The study examines respiratory ED visits specifically for asthma, which falls under respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) uses case time series analysis (a variant of time-series design), (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CI (1.43% increase per 10 μg/m³ increment, 95% CI: 1.34%, 1.52% for respiratory hospitalizations), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports separate results for respiratory hospitalizations which is the outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (COPD) as the outcome, provides a quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (1.6% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95% CI: 0.6%, 2.7%), and appears to be published in English.

This study fails multiple inclusion criteria: (1) it is a meta-analysis, not an original epidemiological study, and (2) the outcome is myocardial infarction (cardiovascular hospitalization), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. The review focuses on respiratory outcomes, making this cardiovascular study ineligible.

This is a systematic review (not an original epidemiological study) examining the association between air pollution and ocular surface disease (conjunctivitis, dry eye, blepharitis), not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. Fails multiple inclusion criteria.

This is a review article (explicitly states 'In this review') focusing on cardiovascular effects and vascular smooth muscle cells, not respiratory hospitalizations. It does not meet inclusion criteria for being an original epidemiological study with respiratory hospitalization outcomes.

This article focuses on cancer outcomes rather than respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. The abstract describes a narrative exploration of PM2.5's carcinogenic effects and proposes mitigation strategies, suggesting this is a review or commentary rather than an original epidemiological study with time-series or case-crossover design. The outcome (cancer) does not match the inclusion criteria requiring respiratory hospitalization/ED visits.

This is explicitly stated as a review article (in both title and abstract). The outcome is cardiac developmental toxicity/congenital heart defects, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. The focus is on gestational exposure and fetal/offspring outcomes, not the required respiratory hospitalization outcomes.

This is explicitly stated to be a review article ('The aim of this review is to provide a brief overview') focusing on in vitro and in vivo experimental studies, not an original epidemiological study. It does not report primary data on respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits, nor does it use time-series or case-crossover design. Reviews are explicitly excluded per the exclusion criteria.

This is explicitly stated as a review article ('This review aims to summarize and discuss...'), not an original epidemiological study. Additionally, the outcomes focus on post-transplant complications (organ rejection, cardiovascular disease, infection-related mortality, vitamin D deficiency) rather than respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits specifically.

This is a review and meta-analysis, not an original epidemiological study. Additionally, the outcome is mortality (not hospitalization/ED visit), and the study design appears to be long-term cohort studies (not time-series or case-crossover). Fails multiple inclusion criteria.

This appears to be a narrative review or commentary article rather than an original epidemiological study. The abstract uses phrases like 'This article discusses' which indicates a review format. While PM2.5 exposure is mentioned and some effect estimates are referenced (8-20% increase), the primary focus is on cardiovascular disease rather than respiratory hospitalizations. The abstract does not describe original data collection, specific study design (time-series or case-crossover), or report specific effect estimates with confidence intervals for respiratory hospitalizations.

This is a viewpoint/commentary article discussing gaps and future directions in air pollution research, not an original epidemiological study. It does not report any quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, etc.) and does not employ a time-series or case-crossover study design. It fails to meet inclusion criterion #1 (original epidemiological study) and criterion #5 (reports effect measure with CI).

This is a meta-analysis, not an original epidemiological study. The outcome is mortality (cardiovascular and respiratory diseases, diabetes), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. The study design does not match the required time-series or case-crossover designs.

This appears to be a review or synthesis of multiple studies rather than an original epidemiological study. The abstract uses phrases like 'Among the analyzed studies' and discusses findings across multiple studies, indicating this is a review article. Additionally, the outcome is mortality (non-accidental, cardiovascular, and respiratory mortality) rather than respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits.

This appears to be a review or commentary article focused on kidney disease outcomes rather than respiratory hospitalizations. The outcome is chronic kidney disease (CKD) and kidney-related mortality, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. The abstract discusses 'emerging epidemiological evidence' and calls for 'more longitudinal studies,' suggesting this is a narrative review rather than an original epidemiological study.

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis (not an original epidemiological study), and the outcome is pregnancy-induced hypertensive disorders (gestational hypertension and preeclampsia), not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. Fails inclusion criteria 1 and 3.

This appears to be a review article ('we critically summarize the literature', 'we discuss the association') focused on cardiovascular disease outcomes rather than respiratory hospitalizations. The primary outcome is cardiovascular disease, stroke, and blood pressure, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits.

This is a systematic review and meta-analysis, not an original epidemiological study. It fails inclusion criterion 1. Additionally, the outcome is infant mortality, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits, failing inclusion criterion 3. The study also examines long-term exposure rather than the acute exposure typically studied in time-series or case-crossover designs.

This is a review article that synthesizes findings from 26 other papers, not an original epidemiological study. The abstract explicitly states 'We reviewed 26 papers' and the title includes 'Effect Estimates, Methodological Challenges, and Future Directions' which is characteristic of a review. This fails inclusion criterion #1.

This is a meta-analysis and systematic review (not an original epidemiological study), and the outcome is cardiac arrhythmia hospitalization/mortality, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. Fails inclusion criteria 1 and 3.

This is a systematic review, not an original epidemiological study. The inclusion criteria specifically require original studies and exclude reviews and meta-analyses. Additionally, the outcome is mortality in people living with HIV, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits.

The study examines ultrafine particles (UFPs, <0.1 μm) rather than PM2.5 (≤2.5 μm). UFPs are a distinct size fraction of particulate matter that is smaller than PM2.5. The study does not report analyzing PM2.5 as an exposure variable, only UFPs and mentions controlling for 'criteria air pollutants' in two-pollutant models. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure of interest.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations (tracheitis) with effect estimates, the primary exposure is Asia dust storm (ADS) events rather than PM2.5 specifically. Although dust storms contain particulate matter, the study does not explicitly analyze PM2.5 as the exposure variable. The abstract does not indicate that PM2.5 was measured or reported as a separate exposure with its own effect estimates.

While this is a time-series study that reports effect estimates with confidence intervals and includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome, the exposure is PM10 (particulate matter <10 μm) from dust storms, not PM2.5 (≤2.5 μm). The abstract explicitly states 'particulate matter <10 μm in diameter' and does not mention PM2.5 measurement or analysis.

The study examines PM10 (particulate matter ≤10 µm) rather than PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm) as the exposure. While the study meets other inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, time-series design, respiratory hospitalizations as outcome, quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals), the exposure does not match the systematic review's requirement for PM2.5 specifically.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with quantitative effect estimates, the exposure is PM10, not PM2.5. The abstract explicitly states the study examined PM₁₀, SO₂ and CO, with no mention of PM2.5 or fine particulate matter ≤2.5 µm. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure.

While this is an original epidemiological study examining respiratory ED visits with a time-series design and quantitative estimates, the exposure is Saharan dust measured by visibility rather than PM2.5 specifically. The abstract does not mention PM2.5 or fine particulate matter measurements. The exposure is characterized only as 'Saharan dust cloud cover' measured through visibility (km), which does not meet the PM2.5 exposure criterion.

While this is a time-series study examining fine particles (likely PM2.5) and asthma hospitalizations, the abstract explicitly states that 'no pollutant alone made a significant contribution to explained variance' and does not report specific effect estimates (RR, OR, or CI) for PM2.5. The study reports only variance explained (R-squared type measures) rather than the required quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals.

The study examines ozone exposure (not PM2.5) and the outcomes are cellulitis (skin infection) and pharyngitis (throat infection), not respiratory hospitalizations. While pharyngitis involves the throat, it is not classified as a respiratory hospitalization outcome for the purposes of this systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

The study examines ultrafine particles (UFP) with diameter <100 nm, not PM2.5 (≤2.5 µm). UFP are much smaller than PM2.5 and represent a different exposure category. While the outcome (respiratory hospitalizations), study design (time-series with Poisson regression), and effect estimates are appropriate, the exposure does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires PM2.5 or fine particulate matter ≤2.5 µm.

The exposure is ozone, not PM2.5. While the study meets other criteria (case-crossover design, ED visits, reports OR with CI), it does not meet the fundamental inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure of interest.

This appears to be a methodological paper proposing a new statistical method (generalized ACE-DLNM) rather than an original epidemiological study. While it applies the method to respiratory hospitalization data as a motivating example, the primary focus is on developing and demonstrating a statistical technique. The abstract emphasizes method development, computational efficiency, and comparison with other statistical approaches rather than reporting epidemiological findings about PM2.5 and respiratory health.

While this study uses GAM models and evaluates air pollution health effects, it does not meet several key inclusion criteria: (1) the study design is described as 'before-after comparative' rather than time-series or case-crossover, (2) the specific exposure (PM2.5) is not explicitly mentioned in the abstract, (3) the outcome is described only as general 'health benefits' without specifying respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits, and (4) no specific effect estimates (RR, OR) are mentioned in the abstract. The study appears to be a policy evaluation rather than a focused epidemiological study on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory emergency room visits (asthma, COPD, pneumonia). It reports multiple relative risks with 95% confidence intervals using generalized additive Poisson regression models. The study is clearly not a review or commentary, and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design (Quasi-Poisson generalized additive model), examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD admissions) as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates (RR = 1.02 with 95% CI) for the association between PM2.5 and hospital admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is asthma emergency department visits which qualifies as respiratory ED visits, (4) it uses a time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) the abstract mentions quantifying associations and reporting ED visit odds, indicating effect estimates are provided, and (6) the publication appears to be in English. While PM2.5 is analyzed alongside other pollutants, this is acceptable per the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design with DLNM, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) outcome is COPD hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 (RR=1.048, 95%CI: 1.030-1.067), and (6) published in English. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design to examine the association between PM2.5 exposure and hospital admissions for respiratory diseases (COPD and respiratory infection). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although cardiovascular outcomes are also examined, the study explicitly includes respiratory hospitalizations as outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (source-specific fine particulate matter), (3) outcome is respiratory disease emergency department visits, (4) study design is time-series (Poisson time-series regression models), (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect measures reported), and (6) published in English in Environmental Health Perspectives. The study examines source-specific PM2.5, which is still PM2.5 exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed (both as a criteria pollutant and through its components SO42-, NO3-, NH4+), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits (asthma/wheeze, bronchitis, pneumonia, URI), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although it examines multiple pollutants in mixture models, PM2.5 is clearly included as an exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed among multiple pollutants, (3) outcome is hospital admission for bronchiectasis which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series study design is clearly stated, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.067, 95%CI 1.020-1.116 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease and hospitalizations for bronchiectasis exacerbations qualify as respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) the outcome is pneumonia hospitalizations which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) it reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR=1.015, 95% CI: 1.010-1.021 for PM2.5), and (5) appears to be published in English. The study examines both PM2.5 and PM10, but PM2.5 is one of the primary exposures analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports percent increases with 95% confidence intervals for multiple age groups, and (6) published in English. Asthma ED visits are a specific type of respiratory emergency department visit.

This is an original epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 exposure and daily respiratory hospitalizations using time-series methods (GAM and DLNM). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (5.4% and 5.8% increases in respiratory hospitalizations per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5). All inclusion criteria are met: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and effect estimates with CIs reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (along with its constituents), (3) includes respiratory hospitalizations as outcomes (specifically pneumonia mentioned with ER% 1.9-5.1%), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess risk percentages with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple health outcomes including cardiovascular, it explicitly reports results for respiratory causes including pneumonia.

This is an original epidemiological study examining fine particulate matter (PM2.5) exposure and respiratory hospitalizations in children. It uses a time-series design (daily counts with Generalized Additive Model with Poisson distribution) and reports quantitative effect estimates (3.8% and 5.6% increased risk). The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with measures of association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for AECOPD, (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (3.5% increase per 10 μg/m³ PM2.5), and (6) published in English. The study examines a specific respiratory condition (COPD exacerbation) requiring ED visits, which falls within the scope of respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

While this study examines respiratory hospitalizations using a case-crossover design and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary exposure is organic carbon (OC) species and their chemical groups (n-alkanes, hopanes, cyclohexanes, PAHs, isoalkanes), not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 is mentioned in the background as context, the actual analysis focuses on specific organic compounds as the exposure of interest. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive model; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures; (3) Outcome is hospital admissions for COPD, a respiratory condition; (4) Time-series design analyzing daily hospital admissions over 2016-2020; (5) Reports percentage change with 95% CI for PM2.5 (2.8%, 95%CI: 1.0-4.7); (6) Published in English. The study specifically excludes ED visits but includes hospitalizations, which satisfies the outcome criterion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 total mass and its components, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with percent increases per IQR (0.5-2.0% and 1.0-2.0% mentioned), and (6) published in English. The study examines PM2.5 and its constituents in relation to respiratory hospitalizations in New York State.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, it uses a cohort design with long-term exposure assessment (1990-2000) rather than the required time-series or case-crossover design. The study follows participants over time and examines long-term average exposures, which is characteristic of a cohort study, not the short-term exposure designs specified in the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine PM2.5 exposure (specifically wildfire smoke PM2.5) and respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits. The study reports odds ratios with confidence intervals for respiratory outcomes including asthma and combined respiratory disease. The exposure is PM2.5, outcomes include both ED visits and hospitalizations for respiratory conditions, and quantitative effect estimates are provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome (along with cardiovascular), and provides quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (posterior intervals) for respiratory hospitalizations. The study reports a 2.57% (95% PI: 0.87%, 4.30%) increase in respiratory hospitalizations per 10-μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 in least-urban counties and 1.13% (0.73%, 1.54%) in most-urban counties.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma hospital admissions (respiratory hospitalization), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants were studied, PM2.5 was specifically analyzed and found to be significantly associated with the outcome.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (aggregated weekly data with GAMs and distributed-lag models) examining the association between fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and COPD hospitalizations. The study reports adjusted relative risks with statistical significance. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization. Although the study examines multiple exposures (weather, influenza, air pollutants), PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as 'fine particulate matter' and analyzed separately.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is non-methane hydrocarbons (NMHC), not PM2.5. PM2.5 is only mentioned as a co-pollutant used for adjustment in two-pollutant models. The study does not report effect estimates for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using distributed lag non-linear models (time-series design); (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) Respiratory ED visits are examined (asthma, COPD, pneumonia, RTI); (4) Time-series design with lag structures; (5) Quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 6.32% increase, 95% CI 4.19-8.49); (6) Published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other PM sizes, PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are clearly analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for asthma, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (1.96%, 95%CI: 0.02, 3.94), and (6) published in English. Asthma ED visits are a respiratory outcome that falls within the scope of respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) the outcome is respiratory disease hospitalization, (4) it uses a time-series study design with generalized additive models, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increase per 10-μg/m³ increment) for PM2.5 and other pollutants, and (6) the abstract is in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

While the primary exposure is ultrafine particles (UFP), the study explicitly states that PM2.5 was analyzed as a co-pollutant and significant positive associations were detected for PM2.5. The study meets all other inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, examines respiratory (asthma) hospitalizations, and reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with 95% CI). The inclusion criteria allow for studies where PM2.5 is one of multiple exposures analyzed.

While this is an original epidemiological study with a case-crossover design examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is ultrafine particles (UFP; <100 nm), not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 is mentioned as an adjustment variable in the analysis, it is not the main exposure of interest. The study focuses on UFP as the exposure, which does not meet the inclusion criteria requiring PM2.5 as the primary exposure.

This is an original time-series study using GAM that examines multiple air pollutants including PM2.5 in relation to respiratory hospitalizations (COPD admissions). Although PM2.5 showed no statistically significant association, it was explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for all pollutants examined, meets the respiratory hospitalization outcome criterion, and is published in English.

This study meets the inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants including NOx and NO2) as an exposure, respiratory hospitalizations and outpatient visits due to bronchitis and asthma as outcomes, uses a time-series design (Poisson regression with daily data), and reports quantitative effect estimates (RR with confidence intervals). Although the abstract emphasizes NO2 results, the study explicitly includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures analyzed, which satisfies the inclusion criterion that PM2.5 can be one of multiple exposures.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is hospital admissions for respiratory disorders (ICD J00-J99), (4) case-crossover design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (2.7% increase per 10 µg·m-3 PM2.5), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from Asian Dust Storms, (3) outcome includes respiratory disease emergency room visits, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR=1.86, 95% CI: 1.30-2.91 for respiratory diseases), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly reports separate effect estimates for respiratory diseases.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and asthma exacerbation requiring healthcare encounters including ED and inpatient settings (hospitalizations). The study reports RR estimates with 95% CIs. While the outcome includes outpatient visits in addition to ED and inpatient encounters, it does capture respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma, which meet the inclusion criteria.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations with reported effect estimates, it uses a cohort study design rather than the required time-series or case-crossover design. The study examines intrauterine exposure during pregnancy and outcomes in infants, which is a different epidemiological approach than the acute exposure-response relationship typically assessed in time-series and case-crossover studies.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure, respiratory (asthma) hospitalizations, uses a time-series design (Poisson regression with DLNM), and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary research question focuses on temperature as the main exposure with PM2.5 as an effect modifier. The study investigates how PM modifies the temperature-asthma relationship rather than examining the direct association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive model for time-series analysis; (2) Exposure includes PM2.5 (along with PM10); (3) Outcome is asthma hospitalization, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with temporal controls); (5) Reports RRs with 95% CIs (RR=1.0156, 95% CI: 1.0055-1.0259 for PM2.5); (6) Published in English. Asthma hospitalization is a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original time-series epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as one of the exposures, (3) respiratory emergency department visits are among the outcomes examined (asthma/wheeze and respiratory disease visits are mentioned), (4) it uses a time-series design with Poisson regression models, (5) the methods indicate associations were estimated with effect measures for interquartile range changes in pollutants, and (6) it is published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and PM2.5 components, the inclusion of respiratory ED visits and PM2.5 as exposures satisfies the review criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory-related hospitalizations, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR per 5 µg/m3 increase in 3-day lag PM2.5: 0.971 (0.885, 1.066) for respiratory hospitalizations), and (6) published in English. The study examines multiple outcomes (respiratory, CVD, all-cause) but respiratory hospitalization is explicitly analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series regression analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (ALRI admissions) as the outcome, and provides a quantitative effect estimate with 95% CI (3.51% increase per 10 μg/m3, 95%CI: 0.96-6.12). The study design, exposure, outcome, and effect measure reporting all align with the systematic review requirements.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using time-series design; (2) Exposure is PM2.5 (fine particulate matter); (3) Outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-10 codes J04.0, J12.0-J18.9, J20.0-J21.9, J45.0); (4) Time-series design explicitly stated; (5) Reports relative risk (RR=1.04) with quantitative effect estimates; (6) Published in English (with Portuguese translation). The study uses generalized additive Poisson regression models and reports RR, proportional attributable risk, and population attributable fraction.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 exposure is analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for COPD, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (6.6% increase, 95% CI 0.5-13.0% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. COPD exacerbation requiring ED visit is a respiratory emergency department outcome.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory (COPD) hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure is major storms and power outages, not PM2.5. PM2.5 is only mentioned as a confounder that was controlled for in the analysis, not as the main exposure of interest. This does not meet inclusion criterion #2 which requires PM2.5 to be the exposure being studied.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is hospital visits for pneumonia which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series study design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates (risk ratios) with 95% confidence intervals are reported (1.3% increase per 10-μg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are analyzed, PM2.5 is specifically included and reported separately.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis with generalized additive mixed models, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from coal mine fire smoke, (3) outcomes include respiratory disease emergency presentations and hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series, and (5) the abstract indicates increased risks were found and associations were examined, suggesting effect estimates were reported. The study appears to be published in English.

While this is a time-series study examining respiratory ED visits with effect estimates, PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is only mentioned as a confounder that was adjusted for, not as a primary exposure of interest. The main exposures analyzed are tree pollen, humidity, and temperature. The study does not report effect estimates for PM2.5 on respiratory outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) It is an original epidemiological study; (2) Exposure includes PM2.5 from wildfire smoke explicitly measured; (3) Outcomes include both respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits; (4) Study design includes case-crossover analysis (bidirectional symmetric design); (5) Reports multiple effect estimates including ORs and RRs with 95% CIs (e.g., OR 1.08 per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 increase for asthma ED visits, RR 1.34 for respiratory ED presentations); (6) Published in English. The study uses appropriate epidemiological methods and provides quantitative estimates of association between PM2.5 and respiratory healthcare utilization.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits as outcomes (specifically for influenza and pneumonia), provides quantitative effect estimates (excess rates) with 95% confidence intervals, and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma and COPD as outcomes, and provides quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals (e.g., 0.4% (0.0%, 0.8%) increase in asthma ED visits per 6.8 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5).

This study meets the key inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory hospital admissions and ambulatory/ED visits, (4) it reports a quantitative effect estimate (1% increase per 10 µg/m³). While the abstract does not explicitly mention confidence intervals or specify whether this is RR/OR, the study design and quantitative reporting suggest effect estimates with uncertainty measures are likely reported in the full text.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory disease hospitalization, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR=1.06, 95% CI: 1.02-1.10 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the study focuses on PM1, it explicitly analyzes PM2.5 effects and provides quantitative estimates for PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (total mass and constituents), (3) includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome, (4) uses time-series analysis design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 3.47% increase with 95% CI: 2.03, 4.94% for respiratory admissions), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly analyzes respiratory hospitalizations which is the outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcomes include respiratory hospitalizations among 214 disease groups studied, (4) time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for hospital admissions per µg/m3 increase in PM2.5, and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple disease outcomes, respiratory diseases are explicitly mentioned as one of the outcomes with positive associations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (among other particulate matter sizes), (3) outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (2.2% increase in risk per 10μg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations, (4) study design is explicitly time-series analysis, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals (e.g., 0.75% increase per 10 μg/m3 with 95% CI), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines circulatory hospitalizations, it separately analyzes and reports results for respiratory hospitalizations, which is the outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) respiratory ED visits are examined as outcomes (asthma, COPD, respiratory infections), (4) time-series study design, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 7.6% increase in asthma visits per 8.2 µg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 5.1-10.1), and (6) published in English. Although the study examines multiple pollutants and both cardiac and respiratory outcomes, it specifically reports PM2.5-respiratory ED visit associations with effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which are respiratory emergency department visits, (4) time-series study design with Poisson regression, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and other pollutants. Although the study found no significant positive associations for PM2.5, it still analyzed PM2.5 exposure and reported effect estimates, making it eligible for inclusion in a systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using Poisson regression on daily hospitalization counts, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) time-series design based on daily counts methodology, (5) reports excess risk percentages with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 4.1% [95% CI, 1.8-6.4] for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines PM2.5 components, PM2.5 itself is analyzed and reported separately.

The study examines cardiovascular outcomes (acute myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, and ischemic stroke) rather than respiratory hospitalizations. Although the study meets other inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, case-crossover design, reports effect estimates with confidence intervals), the outcome does not match the systematic review's focus on respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits.

The study examines coarse particulate matter (PM2.5-10), which refers to particles between 2.5 and 10 micrometers in diameter, not PM2.5 (fine particulate matter ≤2.5 µm). This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 exposure. While the study design (case-crossover), outcome (respiratory hospitalizations), and effect estimates with confidence intervals are appropriate, the exposure is explicitly coarse particles, not PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure along with other pollutants, (3) outcome is emergency department visits for pediatric asthma (respiratory condition), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR IQR=1.03, 95% CI 1.02-1.04 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure from wildfires, reports respiratory emergency department visits as outcomes, provides quantitative effect estimates (ORs with 95% CIs) for respiratory outcomes including asthma/wheeze and COPD, and uses conditional logistic regression appropriate for case-crossover analysis.

The primary exposure is ozone (O3), not PM2.5. Although the abstract mentions that fine particulate matter was included in copollutant models, the study's main focus is on ozone exposure and its association with asthma ED visits. This does not meet the inclusion criterion requiring PM2.5 as the primary exposure of interest.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using appropriate time-series methodology (GAM with DLNM) and reports quantitative effect estimates, the primary outcome is hospitalization COSTS rather than hospitalization occurrence or counts. The study quantifies the effect of air pollution on the economic burden (costs) of hospitalizations, not on the risk or rate of respiratory hospitalizations themselves. This does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visit as the outcome.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (COPD admissions). It uses a time-series design with Poisson regression, reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.25, 95% CI=1.22-1.27 for spring; RR=1.24, 95% CI=1.23-1.26 for winter), and meets all inclusion criteria. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design), it does not report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. The study only reports correlation coefficients (R values) and regression coefficients from a linear model, not the standardized effect estimates (RR/OR) required for systematic review inclusion.
